summary: Defines the IMAP METADATA extension, which lets clients and servers keep annotations on mailboxes or on the whole server, such as a comment on a mailbox's purpose or a message of the day. This is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This lets you stick little notes on mailbox folders, and the mail server can keep them for you.

questions: how to store annotations on imap mailboxes
difference between private and shared imap annotations
how to set a comment on an imap mailbox
subtitle: Sticky notes for IMAP: attach named annotations to a mailbox, or to the whole server.

tldr.problem: IMAP clients had no standard way to store small pieces of data, like a comment, on a mailbox or on the server itself.
tldr.mechanism: The METADATA extension adds GETMETADATA and SETMETADATA commands and a METADATA response, working on slash-separated entry names such as /shared/comment and /private/comment.
tldr.outcome: Clients and servers can share per-mailbox and server-wide annotations, with private entries kept per user and shared entries visible to authorized users.

today: RFC 5464 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What METADATA Adds to IMAP
sections.content:
The METADATA extension lets clients set and retrieve annotations (also called metadata) on an IMAP server. Annotations can belong to a specific mailbox or to the server as a whole. The RFC's examples are a comment about the purpose of a mailbox and a "message of the day" with server status.

A server that supports both kinds announces METADATA in its CAPABILITY response. A server that supports only server annotations announces METADATA-SERVER. The extension adds two commands, SETMETADATA and GETMETADATA, one untagged METADATA response and a METADATA response code.
sections.plainLanguage: IMAP is how your mail program talks to your mail server. This adds a way to attach notes to folders, or to the server itself.

sections.title: Entries, Names and Values
sections.content:
An annotation is a uniquely named entry that has a value. The name is hierarchical, with parts separated by /. A name MUST NOT contain two consecutive slashes or end with a slash, MUST NOT contain an asterisk or a percent sign, and MUST NOT contain non-ASCII characters. Names are case-insensitive, and an invalid name gets a BAD response.

A value is NIL (no value), or a string or binary data of zero or more octets. Multi-line strings use CRLF line ends.

The first part of the name sets the scope. /private entries are stored per user and hidden from others. /shared entries have a single value that authorized users can read and change. A mailbox annotation is addressed by giving the mailbox name, and a server annotation by giving the empty string as the mailbox name.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note has a label like a folder path. Notes in the private pile are only for you. Notes in the shared pile can be read by everybody who is allowed.

sections.title: Defined Entry Names
sections.content:
New entry names MUST be defined in a Standards Track or IESG-approved Experimental RFC, or fall under the vendor namespace. This RFC defines a small starting set.

  • /shared/comment on the server: a shared note for authorized users.
  • /shared/admin on the server: how to contact the administrator. The value MUST be a URI, such as a mailto: or tel: URL, and the entry is always read-only.
  • /shared/comment and /private/comment on a mailbox: a shared or per-user note.
  • /shared/vendor/<vendor-token> and /private/vendor/<vendor-token>: space for a vendor's own annotations. The vendor token MUST be registered with IANA using the ACAP vendor subtree registry.

Entry names normally have at least 2 components, but vendor entries have at least 4.
sections.plainLanguage: There are a few official labels, like "comment", and vendors get their own labelled shelf for their own special notes.

sections.title: GETMETADATA, SETMETADATA and the METADATA Response
sections.content:
GETMETADATA takes a mailbox name, optional options and an entry list, and the server answers with an untagged METADATA response before the tagged OK. Options include MAXSIZE, which skips values larger than the given octet size and reports the biggest skipped size in a [METADATA LONGENTRIES n] code, and DEPTH, which accepts 0, 1 or infinity to also return entries below the named one. Without DEPTH the default is 0.

SETMETADATA sets a list of entry-value pairs, replacing or adding values. A client uses NIL to remove an entry. If any one entry fails, the server MUST NOT change the others. Failures return a tagged NO with a code: MAXSIZE (value too large), TOOMANY (limit on number of annotations reached) or NOPRIVATE (private annotations not supported on that mailbox). Both commands are only available in authenticated or selected state.

A server that supports the ENABLE extension may send unsolicited METADATA responses when a third party changes an annotation, but only after the client enabled METADATA or METADATA-SERVER. These responses contain entry names only, not values, so the client must fetch values again with GETMETADATA.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask the server "what does the note on my Inbox say?" or tell it "write this note on my Inbox". If someone else changes a note, the server can tap you on the shoulder, and you ask again for the new text.

sections.title: Server Behavior and Limits
sections.content:
Servers SHOULD move a mailbox's annotations when the mailbox is renamed, and copy them when INBOX is renamed so INBOX keeps its annotations. They SHOULD delete a mailbox's annotations when it is deleted, so a new mailbox with the same name does not inherit them. Annotations SHOULD be allowed on all types of mailboxes, including those reported as \Noselect.

Servers may limit annotation size and count, but MUST accept values of at least 1024 bytes and at least 10 annotations per server or mailbox. Some annotations may be read-only or computed, for example a total message size that changes as messages come and go.

Support for shared annotations is REQUIRED while support for private annotations is OPTIONAL, because private ones add complexity such as tracking ownership and per-user quota. Without the ACL extension, mailbox annotations need a mailbox the user can see in LIST or LSUB and read or write access to its messages. With ACL, the user needs the l right and any one of r, s, w, i or p. Otherwise the server MUST respond NO.
sections.plainLanguage: The notes travel with their folder when it is renamed and are thrown away when the folder is. The server promises to hold at least a small number of notes of a decent size.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The IMAP security considerations apply for protecting annotations from snooping, and servers MAY support the extension only after a privacy layer has been negotiated. Annotations can hold arbitrary data of varying size, so servers MUST enforce size limits to stop one user from using up all the space. Clients MUST treat annotation values as untrusted, since they could contain malicious content.

Annotations meant to stay private MUST be stored only under the /private prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not trust a note just because it is on your folder, and keep secrets in the private pile only.

sections.title: IANA Registration of Entries
sections.content:
All entries MUST start with /shared or /private. Each registration MUST give a content-type, with a charset where applicable. The template asks for the type (Mailbox or Server), name, description, content-type, RFC number and a contact.

This RFC registers the server entries /shared/comment and /shared/admin and the mailbox entries /shared/comment and /private/comment, all as text/plain; charset=utf-8.
sections.plainLanguage: A public list records the official note labels so that nobody uses the same label for different things.
